:::note[Written against main]
This page follows `main` at a0a88af, and it differs from the copy in HotLoop Cascade 0.1.0-rc.8, the latest release. Parts of it may be newer than what you have installed. The [release notes](/releases/) say what moved.
:::

Two ways to run it. Both want Podman 5.0 or newer and a root install, so they
start at boot with nobody logged in. Both follow
`ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-cascade:stable`, run it read-only and nonroot with
every capability dropped, and let systemd restart it. Updates and how they
roll back are at the end.

## One box, SQLite

`hotloop-cascade.container` and `hotloop-cascade-data.volume`. The database is
a file in the volume, next to the key that seals stored credentials.

```sh
sudo cp hotloop-cascade.container hotloop-cascade-data.volume /etc/containers/systemd/
sudo install -D -m 600 /dev/null /etc/hotloop-cascade/cascade.env
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start hotloop-cascade
```

Open `http://this-box:8080`. The first person to open it makes the first
account, so do that before you share the address.

## PostgreSQL, a server and workers

`postgres/`. The database, the server and, if you want them, more workers.
Postgres is the queue, so the workers take work from the same place. The
database sits on a network of its own and publishes no port.

Three secrets first, made once. The commands are at the top of
`postgres/hotloop-cascade.container`. The key one matters most: lose it and
every stored credential is unreadable. Keep a copy somewhere that is not this
box.

```sh
cd postgres
sudo cp hotloop-cascade.network hotloop-cascade-db.container hotloop-cascade-db.volume \
  hotloop-cascade-data.volume hotloop-cascade.container /etc/containers/systemd/
sudo install -D -m 600 /dev/null /etc/hotloop-cascade/cascade.env
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start hotloop-cascade
```

More workers: `hotloop-cascade-worker.container`. Workers share the data
volume, so they have to be on the same box. Past one box, use the Helm chart.

## Settings

`/etc/hotloop-cascade/cascade.env`, one `NAME=value` per line, and it has to
exist even if it is empty (the `install` line makes it). The ones you will want:

| Setting | What it does |
|---|---|
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_PUBLIC_URL` | The address people reach it at. Webhook and OAuth callback links are built from it. Until you set it, it is `http://localhost:8080`, which only works from the box itself. |
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_METRICS_TOKEN` | Requires `Authorization: Bearer` on `/metrics`. |
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_FILES_DIR` | Turns on the file steps, in this directory. Mount it into the container too. |

The units set only the data directory, the ports and the key, and a value set in a
unit beats one in the env file, so leave those alone. After a change:
`sudo systemctl restart hotloop-cascade`.

## Checking it

```sh
sudo podman healthcheck run hotloop-cascade
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/readyz
sudo podman exec hotloop-cascade /usr/local/bin/hotloop-cascade workflows import - < workflow.yaml
```

Health and metrics are on port 8081, published on the loopback only. If
something else already uses 8080 or 8081, change the left side of the
`PublishPort=` lines.

## Upgrading

The app units follow `:stable` and carry `AutoUpdate=registry`. Turn Podman's
timer on once per box:

```sh
sudo systemctl enable --now podman-auto-update.timer
sudo podman login ghcr.io      # the registry is private; without this the pull fails
```

When it fires, Podman pulls `:stable`, and if the digest changed it restarts the
unit on the new image. The unit is not counted as started until the container
passes its health check (`Notify=healthy`; the check is the binary asking its own
`/readyz`, as a JSON array because the image has no shell). If the new image
never gets there, Podman puts the previous one back under `:stable` and starts
that. The wait is up to 15 minutes, because a new image migrates the database on
its way up.

To hold updates until you say, leave the timer off and run
`sudo podman auto-update` when you are ready. To let them happen only in a
window, install `update-window.conf` (its header says how).

Two things a rollback can't undo. Migrations only go forward, so take a backup
before you turn updates on. A release that changes a table in a way the old one
can't read says so in its release notes. And the database: its image is pinned
to an exact tag and carries no update label, on purpose. A new server image that
can't start is undone by putting the old image back, and a new database image
can start, change the data directory, and only then turn out to be a mistake.
Within PostgreSQL 18 that is an edit to the tag, after the release notes and a
backup.

In the PostgreSQL flavour the server and each worker are separate units, so an
update that can't start rolls back that one unit and not the one beside it.

## What was tried

The units were run for real on Podman 6.1.3, rootless under systemd, with a
local registry standing in for ghcr.io and the shipped units unedited except
for host ports. Standalone and PostgreSQL both: a first start that waits for a
healthy container; an update to a new digest, which came back healthy with the
data intact and, in the PostgreSQL flavour, the database container untouched;
and an update to an image that exits at start, which `podman auto-update`
reported as `rolled back`, with the previous digest running healthy again and
the earlier workflow still running. As a root install on Podman 4.9.3 the
earlier version of the units started and restarted under systemd; the update
path was not run there, and `Notify=healthy` is not honored by 4.9 Quadlet,
which is why the units also carry `--sdnotify=healthy`.

Then both flavours again as a root install, which is how the units say to run
them, on Podman 5.8.7 under systemd in a throwaway privileged container, with
the same local registry standing in for ghcr.io as a mirror and the units
unedited. Standalone: the start waited for a healthy container, a killed
container came back healthy, an update to a good image came up healthy on the
new digest, an update to an image that exits at start was reported
`rolled back` with the good one running again, and a workflow ran after each.
PostgreSQL, with the server and one extra worker: `systemctl start` on the
server held until the database and then the server were healthy, a killed
server came back, an update to a good image moved the server and the worker and
left the database container alone, an update to an image that exits at start
came back `rolled back` with both on the good image again and the database
still untouched, and a workflow ran before, between and after. One thing to
know when you read that output: the server and the worker share one image, and
when the first of them rolled back the other showed `true` instead, with a
restart, and it ended up on the good image anyway. Which one rolls back first
changed from run to run.

Not run: a real Raspberry Pi, and a real ghcr.io pull (the registry is private
and needs `podman login`).
